Nvidia Rival’s CEO on TSMC: “I Would Buy That Stock Every Day of the Week”
Gian Estrada

AVGO

Nvidia Rival's CEO on TSMC: "I Would Buy That Stock Every Day of the Week" ©@Aaron Hawkins from Getty Images via Canva, @genkur from Getty Images via Canva
Key Takeaways

Fractile CEO Walter Goodwin, who is building chips to compete with Nvidia, called TSMC "cheap at the price."

Nvidia's challengers need the same TSMC capacity, so TSMC benefits whichever of them gains share.

TSMC trades at 16.5x forward earnings, below its five-year average, and its main risk is an AI spending slowdown across several big customers.

Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing (TSM:NYSE) makes the chips for Nvidia (NVDA:NASDAQ) and the rivals investors bought after Nvidia announced Jensen Huang's resignation on Nov. 12. That day Nvidia fell, while AMD (AMD:NASDAQ) and Broadcom (AVGO:NASDAQ) rose.

Someone building chips to take on Nvidia has a different favorite. On the 20VC podcast, Harry Stebbings asked Walter Goodwin, founder and CEO of chip startup Fractile, which of his suppliers he'd invest in. Goodwin picked TSMC: "It is cheap at the price. I would buy that stock every day of the week."

Every Challenger Needs the Same Factory

Goodwin's reason is practical. New chip entrants face "a real challenge" in "accessing, for instance, TSMC capacity, HBM capacity," he said. Of the custom AI chips he listed, including OpenAI's, he added: "All of those are rumored to be using Broadcom, for instance. Same or very similar TSMC process nodes, same HBM technology."

So if chip orders shift from Nvidia to AMD or Broadcom-built designs, TSMC still makes the chips.

TSMC Can't Make Enough

TSMC's October revenue rose 59.7% from a year earlier to a record NT$586.9 billion (about US$17.8 billion), and analysts expect revenue to keep climbing:

TSM Revenue, Actual and Consensus Estimates: 2023-2028 (TIKR)

Consensus takes revenue from $120.6 billion in 2025 to $294.5 billion in 2028, 2.44 times as much. Huang's exit doesn't change how many wafers an AI chip needs, whoever designs it.

Full fabs show up in the margin:

TSM Gross Margin: 2021-2025 (TIKR)

Gross margin reached 66.4% in the third quarter of 2026, well above management's long-term target of 56% or higher. TSMC has credited high utilization and cost improvements for the gains.

Nvidia Is Still the Customer That Matters Most

TSMC's largest customer, which it doesn't name, was 19% of 2025 revenue, up from 12% in 2024, and Nvidia is widely reported to be that customer. If Nvidia ordered more than it can sell, TSMC would feel it in future orders.

Share shifts between chip designers matter less to TSMC than to the designers. The bigger risk is an AI spending slowdown, which would likely hit several of its big customers together. Nvidia reports on Nov. 17, and its outlook is the next read on those orders.

title: 3 Beaten-Down Stocks Under $10 to Buy in November

3 Beaten-Down Stocks Under $10 to Buy in November
Steven Porrello, The Motley Fool

^GSPC

Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

It's almost the middle of November. And boy, oh boy -- what a month it's been.

However you slice it, the market has been tinged with volatility. Just look at the S&P 500 (SNPINDEX:^GSPC): The index suffered a huge sell-off in the post-election days of uncertainty, only to stage a quick and powerful recovery a few days later. Meanwhile, AI's biggest winners -- Nvidia, Micron Technology, and Advanced Micro Devices, to name a few -- have also taken a beating, with investors growing worried about inflation and valuations at the same time.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 16x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

Sharp declines, in general, can create buying opportunities for patient and perspicacious investors, but not every beaten-down stock will be a genuine bargain. In particular, I'm looking at growth stocks in emerging industries, many of which have sustained heavy damage in 2026. If you're willing to stomach the volatility, the following three growth stocks might be worth a closer look.

Image source: Getty Images.

1. Archer Aviation

Archer Aviation (NYSE:ACHR) is one of the frontrunners in the emerging electric air taxi market. Its Midnight aircraft, which can take off and land vertically like a helicopter, could offer travelers a way to soar over congested roads in cities around the world.

Earlier in 2026, Archer entered the fourth and final stage of the FAA type certification, the completion of which would bring it one step closer to launching commercial passenger services. The company eked out about $5 million in third-quarter revenue, while also sustaining a hefty $275 million loss that same quarter. These losses are heavy, but it is arguably the price Archer must pay to launch its novel eVTOL (electric vertical takeoff and landing) technology.

Despite its losses, Archer has been making good progress. Recently, it received FAA authorization to begin piloted demonstrations of Midnight in Los Angeles, where it will serve as the official air taxi provider for the 2028 Olympics. It's also in the midst of acquiring three subsidiaries from Boeing, one of which generates more than $200 million in annual revenue.

2. Joby Aviation

Like Archer, Joby Aviation (NYSE:JOBY) is developing electric air taxis for urban transportation. It is, however, farther along than Archer in the FAA's certification process, having already begun testing in the fifth and final stage of its certification process (Joby reports its progress in five stages, while Archer uses four phases).

AMD's Two Catalysts Gain Momentum

IO Fund said AMD's two strategic product launches, which is the company's lineup of Venice server CPUs and Helios MI400-series AI accelerators, are exceeding the chipmaker's initial expectations.

The firm had highlighted AMD management's expectations for server CPU revenue to grow more than 70% in 2027, while overall Data Center revenue was expected to grow "well over 100%."

title: Nvidia Fell While AMD and Broadcom Jumped. Here’s What History Says Happens Next to All 3  Stocks.
detail:
Nvidia Fell While AMD and Broadcom Jumped. Here’s What History Says Happens Next to All 3 Stocks.
Keithen Drury, The Motley Fool
Sat, November 14, 2026 at 4:55 PM EST 5 min read
NVDA
AMD
AVGO
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

Nvidia (NASDAQ:NVDA) shareholders have had a rough few weeks. Nvidia's stock was a bit weak heading into November amid a marketwide AI sell-off, but in the days since news broke that its CEO, Jensen Huang, had an affair with an alleged Chinese spy, the stock has taken a beating. That weakness has continued after Huang's announcement on Thursday that he was stepping down from the CEO role. CFO Colette Kress has been tapped to lead the company on an interim basis while the board searches for the next CEO.

Some companies' losses are others' gains, and while Nvidia is down 21% so far this month, AMD (NASDAQ:AMD) has risen by around 4% and Broadcom (NASDAQ:AVGO) is up about 6%. That's a major mismatch, but the question is: What happens next with this trio of chipmakers?

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 16x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

Let's take a look at what history has to say about what's going on, and consider which stock may be the best to buy of this trio right now.

Image source: Getty Images.

Nvidia is a major wild card

These three companies are all competitors in the data center computing world. Nvidia and AMD design GPUs, which are broad-purpose computing units that excel at handling a wide range of computationally heavy workloads. However, that flexibility comes at a cost. GPUs are more expensive to manufacture, buy, and operate than chips that are purpose-built for narrow types of AI workloads. That's where Broadcom's application-specific integrated circuits (ASICs) come in — those custom AI chips are becoming quite popular with data center operators.

Nvidia has by far the largest data center segment of the three. During its most recently reported quarter, its data center revenue rose 117% year over year to $89 billion. Broadcom's AI semiconductor division is far smaller, with quarterly revenue of $16.7 billion. However, it was growing at a much faster 221% year-over-year pace.

AMD is in last place among the three. Its data center revenues grew at a "slower" 97% year-over-year pace to $8.5 billion.

However, if Nvidia's market leadership slips, AMD would likely have the most to gain. Broadcom's chips are becoming increasingly popular, but they can't do everything a GPU can.

Huang has resigned, and the question now is: How well can Nvidia survive without him? While he was deeply involved in the details of the operation and the loss of his leadership will be a blow to the company, there are likely numerous people who could succeed him and keep Nvidia on track. Companies go through CEO transitions all the time without getting derailed — even when (as in this case) there's no clear succession plan in place.

AMD outperformed Nvidia by 53.2 percentage points over five trading days, according to The Kobeissi Letter. That is the widest gap between the two chipmakers since Nvidia went public in January 1999.

That lead met its first test on Friday, when AMD stock fell 8.75%. Nvidia's November 17 earnings report now sets up the next one.

How Nvidia's Leadership Crisis Fed the AMD Rally

AMD rallied 44.7% over the 5-day stretch while Nvidia dropped 8.5%, according to The Kobeissi Letter. The previous record gap, set in April 2016, stood at 49.9 percentage points.

So far this year, the AMD vs Nvidia gap is even wider. AMD stock has gained 149.4% since January 1, while Nvidia is down 12.7%, as of Friday's close. That puts the year-to-date gap at about 162 percentage points.

Follow us on X to get the latest news as it happens

The run overlapped with growing scrutiny of Jensen Huang, who quit Nvidia as CEO on November 12. The company named CFO Colette Kress interim CEO while its board searches for a permanent replacement.

AMD also gave buyers its own numbers to work with. Its third-quarter revenue rose 45% from a year earlier to a record $13.4 billion. Data center sales nearly doubled to $8.5 billion.

"AMD has been a major beneficiary of Nvidia's historic volatility," The Kobeissi Letter posted on X.

Friday's Sell-Off Hands the Next Move to Nvidia

The record run lost some ground in Friday's session. AMD closed at $534.06, down from $585.30, and slipped another 2.41% to $521.20 after hours.

AMD Stock Performance. Source: Google Finance

Chip stocks sold off as a group. The 10-year Treasury yield remained above 5% after October's producer price index. Rising yields tend to hit growth stocks hardest, since their value rests on profits expected years ahead.

Trading volume reached 48.6 million shares, nearly double the 3-month average. Analysts at The Motley Fool linked part of the drop to profit-taking after the surge.

The after-hours price now sits just above $514. BeInCrypto's AMD stock price analysis marked that level as the line that would break the bullish setup.

Nvidia earnings land on Tuesday after the US market closes. The company guided for $108 billion in third-quarter revenue, plus or minus 2%. Analysts polled by LSEG expect about $109.2 billion and adjusted earnings of $2.48 per share.

The quarter closed on October 25, before Huang resigned, so the results will reflect his tenure. The guidance for the next quarter will be the first issued with Kress as interim CEO.

Solid results and guidance could draw investors back to Nvidia. A weak one could drag the whole chip group lower, AMD included, because Friday showed both stocks still trade together.
